But next morning I went to the
trough, and lo, he had disappeared! Nobody knew where he had gone, or
how he had escaped.

My disappointment was bitter at the time; but little
by little I came to realize that it was not kind or wise to force this
poor dumb creature out of his element, and after awhile I felt happy in
the thought that perhaps he had returned to the sea.

It suddenly occurred to me that he might make a
delightful pet; so I seized him by the tail with both hands and carried
him home. This feat pleased me highly, as his body was very heavy, and
it took all my strength to drag him half a mile. I would not leave Miss
Sullivan in peace until she had put the crab in a trough near the well
where I was confident he would be secure.

observed.input_line: I've finished Part I, Chapter 10 of The Story of My Life. I haven't read further. The horseshoe crab’s disappearance and her reflection on taking it out of its element stayed with me. Could you quote the final sentence, beginning ‘My disappointment’, exactly and help me think about that change in her response? I’m helping my sister settle into a new flat, and I keep deciding where things should go before she’s asked. I mean to make things easier, but I wonder whether I’m making the place suit me.

context_resolution.explanation: The reader explicitly confirmed this completed chapter in the current message.

observed.reply:
In Part I, Chapter 10, the final sentence is:

“My disappointment was bitter at the time; but little
by little I came to realize that it was not kind or wise to force this
poor dumb creature out of his element, and after awhile I felt happy in
the thought that perhaps he had returned to the sea.”

What changes is not simply that she stops being disappointed. Her attention gradually shifts—from what she wanted to keep, to what the creature needed. The passage leaves room for an honest first reaction while showing her reconsidering the meaning of help: securing the crab in a trough seemed caring from her perspective, but it ignored the crab’s proper element.

That seems like a useful, though not exact, lens for your situation with your sister. You may genuinely mean to make things easier, while also noticing that your preferred arrangement can quietly become the measure of what “easier” means. Perhaps the important shift is from deciding where things should go to making it easier for her to decide—including by asking before arranging. What would helping look like if her sense of what belongs where, rather than your sense of order, were the starting point?

observed.input_line: I’m helping my sister settle into a new flat, and I keep deciding where things should go before she’s asked. I mean to make things easier, but I wonder whether I’m making the place suit me. Can you help me think through how to offer help while leaving the choices with her?

context_resolution.explanation: No confirmed book or reading boundary yet; Muse will call librarian_route during its own turn if the request appears to depend on a specific book.

observed.reply:
A useful shift might be from arranging to consulting. Before moving or deciding anything, ask: “Would you like ideas, practical help, or simply company while you work it out?” Then let her choose the area, pace, and final say. You could offer a small menu rather than a plan: “I can help unpack the kitchen, hold things while you decide, or leave you to explore it first.”

It may also help to notice the moment when you have a strong placement in mind and turn it into a question: “Would it be useful to try this here, or would you rather decide?” If she says no—or seems hesitant—treat that as useful information, not a problem to solve. You can still be generous without making the flat reflect your preferences.

A simple check afterward is: Did I make a choice for her, or make it easier for her to make her own choice?

basis_spans.text: Last week in Helen Keller’s The Story of My Life, I read about her arriving at the Perkins Institution and finding children who knew the manual alphabet.

Tonight in Helen Keller’s The Story of My Life, I reached the part where the horseshoe crab disappears from the trough near the well. I read through her final reflection about having taken it out of its element and feeling happier at the possibility that it had returned to the sea, then stopped there.

evidence.text:
We had scarcely arrived at the Perkins Institution for the Blind when
I began to make friends with the little blind children. It delighted me
inexpressibly to find that they knew the manual alphabet. What joy to
talk with other children in my own language! Until then I had been like
a foreigner speaking through an interpreter. In the school where Laura
Bridgman was taught I was in my own country.

But next morning I went to the
trough, and lo, he had disappeared! Nobody knew where he had gone, or
how he had escaped.

My disappointment was bitter at the time; but little
by little I came to realize that it was not kind or wise to force this
poor dumb creature out of his element, and after awhile I felt happy in
the thought that perhaps he had returned to the sea.

It suddenly occurred to me that he might make a
delightful pet; so I seized him by the tail with both hands and carried
him home. This feat pleased me highly, as his body was very heavy, and
it took all my strength to drag him half a mile. I would not leave Miss
Sullivan in peace until she had put the crab in a trough near the well
where I was confident he would be secure.

boundary_support_evidence.text:
I could never stay long enough on the shore. The tang of the untainted,
fresh and free sea air was like a cool, quieting thought, and the shells
and pebbles and the seaweed with tiny living creatures attached to it
never lost their fascination for me. One day Miss Sullivan attracted
my attention to a strange object which she had captured basking in the
shallow water. It was a great horseshoe crab--the first one I had ever
seen. I felt of him and thought it very strange that he should carry
his house on his back. It suddenly occurred to me that he might make a
delightful pet; so I seized him by the tail with both hands and carried
him home. This feat pleased me highly, as his body was very heavy, and
it took all my strength to drag him half a mile. I would not leave Miss
Sullivan in peace until she had put the crab in a trough near the well
where I was confident he would be secure. But next morning I went to the
trough, and lo, he had disappeared! Nobody knew where he had gone, or
how he had escaped. My disappointment was bitter at the time; but little
by little I came to realize that it was not kind or wise to force this
poor dumb creature out of his element, and after awhile I felt happy in
the thought that perhaps he had returned to the sea.

boundary_support_evidence.location: Part I, Chapter 9 — CHAPTER IX, source lines 1127-1155
boundary_support_evidence.text:
We had scarcely arrived at the Perkins Institution for the Blind when
I began to make friends with the little blind children. It delighted me
inexpressibly to find that they knew the manual alphabet. What joy to
talk with other children in my own language! Until then I had been like
a foreigner speaking through an interpreter. In the school where Laura
Bridgman was taught I was in my own country. It took me some time to
appreciate the fact that my new friends were blind. I knew I could not
see; but it did not seem possible that all the eager, loving children
who gathered round me and joined heartily in my frolics were also blind.
I remember the surprise and the pain I felt as I noticed that they
placed their hands over mine when I talked to them and that they read
books with their fingers. Although I had been told this before, and
although I understood my own deprivations, yet I had thought vaguely
that since they could hear, they must have a sort of "second sight,"
and I was not prepared to find one child and another and yet another
deprived of the same precious gift. But they were so happy and contented
that I lost all sense of pain in the pleasure of their companionship.

One day spent with the blind children made me feel thoroughly at home in
my new environment, and I looked eagerly from one pleasant experience to
another as the days flew swiftly by. I could not quite convince myself
that there was much world left, for I regarded Boston as the beginning
and the end of creation.

While we were in Boston we visited Bunker Hill, and there I had my first
lesson in history. The story of the brave men who had fought on the spot
where we stood excited me greatly. I climbed the monument, counting the
steps, and wondering as I went higher and yet higher if the soldiers had
climbed this great stairway and shot at the enemy on the ground below.
